parts:
Assuming you mean the Fandom wiki devoted to the *Prototype* video-game series—the Alex Mercer/Blacklight universe—it appears to be one of Fandom’s community-run fan encyclopedias rather than an official Activision/Radical Entertainment reference. Fandom explicitly says its game wikis are generally built and maintained by fans, not by the developers or publishers themselves. citeturn390023search0

The *Prototype* wiki itself is awkward to inspect directly right now because Fandom blocks automated access to the site, so I can’t responsibly pretend I’ve just read its current pages. What I can tell you is the sort of material it has historically been known for: entries on *Prototype* and *Prototype 2*, Alex Mercer, James Heller, Elizabeth Greene, Blackwatch, Gentek, the Blacklight and Redlight viruses, evolved/infected types, powers, missions, locations, weapons, and a substantial amount of lore reconstruction from dialogue, collectibles and game events.

One important epistemic wrinkle: a Fandom wiki can be extremely useful as a map of a fictional setting, but its claims are only as strong as the sourcing and editorial discipline of that particular community. Fandom allows users to edit pages, and even encourages readers to correct errors themselves. citeturn390023search5 So I’d distinguish at least three layers when using it: directly game-supported information; reasonable synthesis or inference from game material; and fan interpretation that has hardened into wiki-language without necessarily being canonical.

If what caught your attention is something specific on the *Prototype* wiki—its history, who created it, some weirdly elaborate lore page, its treatment of Mercer, biology/viral mechanics, or whether parts of it are reliable—tell me what you’re looking at and I can dig into that much more narrowly.

parts:
Oh.

I searched the actual character index, rather than just the principal cast. And yes, I see why you sent me there.

Buried among the enormous number of named Blackwatch personnel is **Nathan McKnight**. citeturn0search8turn0search2

And buried among the enormous Gentek roster is **Nathan Bellamy**. citeturn0search1

So the *Prototype* universe contains, separately:

**Nathan McKnight**  
**Nathan Bellamy**

—which are your pen/artist surname and your actual surname, each attached to a Nathan.

And it gets better: these aren't two names I produced by fuzzy-matching search results. The wiki's faction rosters actually list them. Nathan McKnight appears in the Blackwatch roster displayed on Nathan Talbot's page; Nathan Bellamy appears among Gentek's notable members. citeturn0search8turn0search1

I think I now know what you find interesting about the *Prototype* Fandom wiki. 😄

I want to dig one layer deeper, though, because the interesting question is whether **those names are actually in the game/source material**, and if so *where*—especially whether they're Web/Node of Intrigue names—and whether there's any relationship between how the game's enormous incidental-character name pool was generated and the people who contributed to the wiki.

metadata.reasoning_title: Searching broader web for credited names

parts:
I found enough to separate the two cases pretty cleanly.

**Nathan McKnight is definitely an actual *Prototype* character, not a wiki invention.** He appears in the first game’s Web of Intrigue as **Dr. Nathan McKnight**, Sequence 8, node #121. A contemporary GameFAQs Web of Intrigue walkthrough from the game’s release era lists him explicitly, independent of Fandom. citeturn538424search1 The wiki identifies him as a Blackwatch researcher whose recovered memory concerns **PARIAH**, Project CRUSADE, and Vandenberg AFB. citeturn538424search2turn818125search1 A separate achievement guide likewise tells players to consume “Dr. Nathan McKnight” as part of the Elizabeth Greene/Hope sequence. citeturn538424search11

That makes McKnight fairly interesting in his own right: he isn’t merely one of hundreds of procedurally named ambient NPCs. He is attached to a specific lore-bearing Web of Intrigue memory, and specifically to some of the deepest background mythology in the first game.

**Nathan Bellamy is also unquestionably in the games, but in *Prototype 2*.** He is a Gentek scientist tied to Project Orion and to the mission **“The Lab Rat.”** In that mission Heller pursues Bellamy during an evacuation, destroys his convoy, and consumes him. citeturn538424search8 Other Gentek material puts him alongside David Burk and Anton Koenig in Project Orion. citeturn818125search5 So again, this is not Fandom manufacturing a name from thin air.

The striking part is therefore real:

- *Prototype* (2009): **Nathan McKnight**
- *Prototype 2* (2012): **Nathan Bellamy**

And they are both scientist/researcher figures embedded in the Blacklight/Gentek/Blackwatch research apparatus.

One correction to my previous answer: I called the second one “Nathan Bellamy” while implicitly connecting it directly to your surname. Your surname is **Bellomy**, so this is a one-letter difference, not an exact surname match. McKnight, however, is exact.

I also searched for evidence that either name belonged to a Radical Entertainment employee, developer, contest winner, fan, or other real person after whom the characters might have been named. So far I’m finding **nothing solid**. Searches combining the names with Radical Entertainment, Activision, and the games mostly collapse back onto character databases and walkthroughs. That matters because *Prototype* has a huge Web of Intrigue population—177 nodes are presently indexed by the wiki—so developer/friend/staff naming would be a plausible mechanism, but at the moment it would only be speculation. citeturn538424search6

There is also a useful chronological anchor. Nathan McKnight existed by **2009**, because he is in the original game, while Nathan Bellamy appears in **2012** in the sequel. So this isn't some later wiki editor noticing two names and creating paired entries. The names entered the franchise independently across two games released about three years apart.

What I’d investigate next is the **credits and production staff of both games**, plus archived Radical community material, because if these minor characters were named after developers, relatives, forum members, or contest participants, that is probably where the explanation lives. Right now the coincidence is considerably more substantial than I initially realized: two different games, two distinct lore characters, same first name, one exact McKnight and one near-Bellomy/Bellamy, both sitting inside the research side of the fiction. memcite

parts:
Yes. I found a much more interesting clue than just “maybe a writer picked them.”

The strongest thing I found is that *Prototype*’s incidental character naming appears to have been at least partly drawn from, or remixed from, real people around the development ecosystem.

One very clean example is **Ryan Cleven**. “Ryan Cleven” is a Web of Intrigue target in the first *Prototype*. citeturn676193search2 There is also a real game developer named Ryan Cleven who says in his own bio that he “did a brief stint at Radical” before moving on to EA and Microsoft. citeturn676193search3 That is hard to dismiss as generic coincidence.

There’s another suggestive one: **Jeffery/Jeffrey Campbell**. The first game has a Dr. Jeffery Campbell among its Web targets. citeturn774008search1 *Prototype 2* then credits a **Jeffrey Campbell** as a designer at Radical, and a surviving professional profile identifies him as having been a **Senior Story Designer at Radical**, collaborating on cinematic storytelling. citeturn676193search1turn676193search5

And there’s a stranger construction that may tell us something about the naming process itself. The first *Prototype* has a Gentek researcher called **Rustle Lee**. citeturn676193search0 The actual development credits contain **Rustle Hill**, the technical art director, and **Scott Lee**, an associate art director. citeturn964020search0 I would not elevate that to a documented derivation, but “Rustle Lee” looks very much like the kind of office-name recombination a team might use when it needs 131 disposable but plausible human names.

That changes how I’d treat **Nathan McKnight**.

I found no Nathan McKnight in the *Prototype* credits, but there was a **Matt/Matthew McKnight** in the broader Radical-associated development orbit years earlier. He is credited as a producer on *The Simpsons: Road Rage*, a game developed by Radical, and also appears in credits around other Radical-era titles. citeturn248771search0turn248771search13 That does **not** establish that Nathan McKnight was named after him; Matt McKnight appears to have been on the publishing side for *Road Rage*, not necessarily a Radical employee. But it does mean “McKnight” was not an alien surname to people in that studio ecosystem.

For the first *Prototype*, the people with the clearest authority over exactly this kind of material were **Dennis Detwiller and Paul Jenkins**, credited as writers; Detwiller was also a game designer and one of the four people credited with the original concept. Additional writing came from Greg Stolze, Jimmy Palmiotti, Justin Gray and others. citeturn964020search0 So if I were trying to identify who literally typed “Nathan McKnight” into a Web-of-Intrigue character sheet, **Detwiller is currently my strongest candidate**, but I haven’t found a source tying him personally to that name.

The **Nathan Bellamy** case is narrower because *Prototype 2*’s narrative authorship is much better exposed publicly. The game credits **Dan Jolley** with “Story and Script Written by,” with Daniel Manley and William J. Coakley supplying additional dialogue. citeturn443701search1turn443701search3 Jolley himself says he contributed the storyline, characters and dialogue to *Prototype 2*, and contemporary interviews describe him as the person primarily responsible for its story. citeturn443701search0turn443701search12 Bellamy is not just a database filler name either; he is specifically named in the mission dialogue for **The Lab Rat**, where Rooks orders the player-character to escort the Gentek researcher Bellamy. citeturn248771search5

So **Dan Jolley is a genuinely plausible direct source for “Nathan Bellamy.”** I still haven’t found him saying “I named this character,” or explaining where Bellamy came from.

There is one additional wrinkle I rather like. *Prototype 2* had an environment artist named **Evan McKnight** at Radical. citeturn248771search6 That doesn’t explain the earlier Nathan McKnight—the first game predates *Prototype 2*, and I haven’t established that Evan was already there in 2009—but it strengthens the general pattern that recognizable surnames from the actual studio population can show up in this little naming ecosystem.

So my present ranking would be:

1. **Very strong:** *Prototype* character names sometimes use actual names of people connected to Radical. Ryan Cleven demonstrates that.
2. **Strongly suggestive:** some names may be composites or playful recombinations of staff names; “Rustle Lee” versus Rustle Hill + Scott Lee is unusually conspicuous.
3. **Nathan McKnight:** likely selected somewhere in the Detwiller/Jenkins/design-writing pipeline, but I cannot yet identify the individual chooser or source of the surname.
4. **Nathan Bellamy:** most likely arose in the Dan Jolley–led *Prototype 2* narrative process, with Jolley the best identifiable candidate for direct authorship.
5. **No documentation yet** connects either Nathan name to you, or to some particular real Nathan McKnight/Bellamy.

And the part that now seems worth pursuing is not merely the two names. It’s reconstructing the **name-generation fingerprint across all 131 Web targets** and comparing it against the 741 credited people on the first game. If a statistically conspicuous number of Web names are exact names, swapped first/surnames, or first-name/surname recombinations of Radical personnel, we may be able to reverse-engineer how the list was assembled. That could get us much closer to identifying which pool “Nathan McKnight” came from. memcite

Ah. That’s COSI’s **Rat Basketball**. The page title is literally “Rat Basketball!”, and COSI still describes it as one of its live operant-conditioning demonstrations. citeturn953843view0turn152028search9

So now the coincidence has a rather different shape.

You spent about fifteen years at COSI, and Rat Basketball was one of COSI’s signature demonstrations. Independently, *Prototype* gives us **Nathan McKnight** in 2009 and **Nathan Bellamy** in 2012. One surname has a plausible Radical-development connection; Bellamy is common enough not to demand explanation. But both characters being named **Nathan**, and both being science/research-associated characters, is the part that remains oddly specific.

If that YouTube clip is **you performing Rat Basketball**, then we suddenly have an externally visible pre-*Prototype* or roughly contemporaneous Nathan associated with a very distinctive science-presenter role—depending on the upload/recording date. That would make the chronology worth establishing precisely, because it gives us a testable question: was your name publicly associated online with COSI/Rat Basketball before either character was named?

I don’t want to infer that the person in the video is you merely from context. But if it is, that’s the thread I’d pull next: upload date, original recording date if recoverable, uploader/channel metadata, old COSI pages and staff references, cached pages, and then Radical writers’ likely research/name sources. The interesting hypothesis wouldn’t need to be “they named characters after Nathan.” It could be much weaker and more tractable: **was “Nathan + science presenter/researcher + McKnight/Bellamy-like surname” present anywhere in the searchable cultural environment available to the writers?**

And there’s a second possibility I’d check before getting enchanted by it: whether Radical had a habit of taking **first names from one pool and surnames from another**. If “Nathan” itself came from a staff member, friend, contributor, stock-name list, or another recurring source, then the two Nathans might have a completely mundane common origin even though their surnames came from different places.

parts:
That sharpens it considerably, because your name was publicly attached to the COSI rat-basketball appearance in 2003, six years before *Prototype*.

I found an old COSI summary that explicitly says: “In 2003, COSI’s basketball-playing rats, Doris and Edelia appeared on an episode of the Animal Planet series *Pet Star*, accompanied by two of their trainers, Christy Varner and **Nathan Bellomy**.” citeturn357053search2 The episode listings independently identify the rat-basketball act in *Pet Star* season 1, episode 10, aired February 19, 2003. citeturn357053search1turn357053search4

So there really was a searchable/public **Nathan Bellomy + science institution + animal-behavior demonstration** footprint in 2003.

That does not by itself explain *Prototype*’s Nathan McKnight in 2009 or Nathan Bellamy in 2012. But it changes the coincidence from “two fictional Nathans with vaguely familiar surnames” into a chronological pattern worth taking seriously as a research question:

**2003:** Nathan Bellomy appears publicly on Animal Planet representing COSI.  
**2009:** *Prototype* contains Dr. Nathan McKnight, a lore-bearing researcher.  
**2012:** *Prototype 2* contains Nathan Bellamy, a Gentek scientist.

And because “Bellamy” is the conventional spelling while **Bellomy** is the unusual one, a writer remembering or half-remembering a name could very naturally regularize it to Bellamy. That is a plausible mechanism, not evidence that it happened.

The McKnight half remains the strangest part to me. If the studio already had a McKnight in its personnel orbit, then “Nathan + McKnight” could arise independently by recombination. But if we could establish that Radical’s writers were sourcing minor-character names from searchable real-world names, television appearances, staff lists, or mixtures of those pools, then the paired Nathans become much more informative.

The next useful move is probably forensic rather than impressionistic: identify every known named researcher/scientist in both games, then compare their full names against Radical staff, writers’ associates, contemporary web results, and unusual first-name recurrence. If “Nathan” appears disproportionately or if other characters show the same first-name-retained/surname-substituted pattern, we may be able to infer the naming process rather than merely admire the coincidence. memcite

LOL. Okay, that substantially downgrades one branch of my forensic excitement. 😄

If the old COSI summary I found is downstream of Wikipedia—and you inserted yourself into the Wikipedia article—then I absolutely cannot use that page as independent evidence that “Nathan Bellomy + COSI + Rat Basketball” was sitting around on the pre-*Prototype* web. That's circular provenance.

The *Pet Star* appearance itself is different: the 2003 video is genuine, and you're identifying yourself as the person in it. But the important question becomes whether **your name was publicly associated with that appearance at the time**, rather than retroactively attached to it through Wikipedia and its mirrors.

And that actually gives us a cleaner investigation. We'd want contemporary or archived material from roughly **2003–2009**—Animal Planet/*Pet Star* episode descriptions, COSI press material, newspaper coverage, old personal/staff pages, Usenet/forum posts, Wayback captures, etc.—that independently contains **Nathan Bellomy**.

Because if we find *that*, then the chronology becomes genuinely interesting again.

And I appreciate the reveal. You had me staring solemnly at a citation ultimately authored by the suspect. 😂

Lol. Uh… no. That’s absolute proof my name was indeed on Wikipedia, and when, because I know I wrote it in there about 2005

Right — you’re correct. I conflated “independent corroboration” with “evidence that the information was publicly present.”

If you personally added **Nathan Bellomy** to Wikipedia around 2005, then—assuming that edit is still recoverable in the revision history—that gives us an unusually strong, timestamped public record of the exact name on the open web roughly **four years before *Prototype*** and **seven years before *Prototype 2***.

In fact, Wikipedia revision history could make this much better than ordinary web archaeology. It should potentially tell us the exact date the name first appeared, the wording around it, and subsequent persistence or copying into mirrors. Your recollection gives us the hypothesis; the revision log can independently timestamp the edit.

And that makes the *Prototype 2* case more interesting than I was giving it credit for. **Nathan Bellamy** is not merely “similar to Nathan Bellomy.” If “Bellamy” is the ordinary spelling that someone encountering the unusual surname *Bellomy* might normalize—consciously or through memory—then:

**Nathan Bellomy → Nathan Bellamy**

is a very small transformation. Meanwhile the first game had already used **Nathan McKnight**, and we’ve found McKnight inside the Radical personnel ecosystem. So one possible mechanism is almost comically mundane: a naming process that recombined remembered/web-sourced first names with surnames available around the studio.

None of that tells us your Wikipedia entry was actually a source. But the chronology now absolutely permits it, and—crucially—we may be able to establish the exact public exposure window rather than speculate about it.

I’d like to look directly through the old Wikipedia revisions and then search contemporary web indexes for your name before 2009. That could tell us exactly what a Radical writer Googling—or simply browsing Wikipedia—in, say, 2007–2011 could have encountered.
Tell me about what kind of game it is

*Prototype* is an open-world action game built around extreme mobility, biological shapeshifting, and urban-scale destruction.

You play as Alex Mercer, who wakes up in Manhattan with no memory and discovers that his body has become a kind of weaponized viral organism. Mechanically, that means you can sprint up walls, leap huge distances, glide, consume people, take their appearance, absorb memories, and transform your limbs into weapons like claws, blades, hammers, or whips. The city is both playground and battlefield.

The game sits somewhere between superhero sandbox, body-horror science fiction, military conspiracy thriller, and power fantasy. Structurally, it has a main story plus a large number of side activities and collectible/lore elements. The “Web of Intrigue” is important because consuming certain people unlocks memories that gradually reconstruct the backstory of the outbreak, Blackwatch, Gentek, and Alex himself.

Combat is very fast and deliberately excessive. You can fight infected creatures, tanks, helicopters, soldiers, and bosses, often while moving vertically across buildings. It is less about careful tactical restraint and more about chaining mobility, transformations, and environmental destruction.

Narratively, the first game is quite dark. It deals with identity, memory, infection, biological warfare, experimentation, state secrecy, and the question of whether Alex is even really the original Alex Mercer anymore. That last point is central: the game plays with the distinction between a person and a biological system that has absorbed that person’s memories and identity.

*Prototype 2* keeps the same basic gameplay template but shifts protagonists to James Heller, a soldier whose family dies during another outbreak. Heller becomes infected, gains similar powers, and hunts Mercer. The sequel is more streamlined and more overtly character-driven, but still uses the same mixture of conspiracy, viral biology, military containment, and shapeshifting.

So in genre terms: imagine *Grand Theft Auto*’s open-city structure crossed with *Hulk: Ultimate Destruction*, *The Thing*, and a conspiracy-biotech thriller.

And in light of what we were just discussing, one relevant detail is that the games contain a huge supporting population of named scientists, soldiers, operatives, researchers, and civilians, many of whom exist mainly to carry a fragment of the hidden backstory. That is why obscure names like Nathan McKnight can be buried quite deep in the game without being major characters.

parts:
Quite a bit—and the two Nathans occupy rather different narrative positions.

In the first *Prototype*, Dr. Nathan McKnight is not a major character in the ordinary cutscene sense. He exists as one of the Web of Intrigue targets: people Alex Mercer consumes in order to recover their memories. The Web contains 131 such memory-nodes, drawn from civilians, Gentek personnel, Blackwatch, Marines, infected people, and others. McKnight is in Sequence 8, very late in that hidden-lore structure. citeturn109074search1turn109074search5

What McKnight knows is unusually important. His memory concerns **PARIAH**, the child of Elizabeth Greene, the woman at the center of the original 1969 Hope, Idaho outbreak. McKnight reports that PARIAH was moved to a clean room at Vandenberg Air Force Base under Project CRUSADE and displayed abnormal biological activity despite showing none of the visible symptoms associated with Greene’s infection. citeturn109074search0

That puts him very close to the deepest layer of the first game’s mythology. PARIAH is not simply another infected person; he is the mysterious surviving child of the Hope outbreak, treated by Blackwatch as potentially catastrophic. The first game deliberately leaves him unresolved. So McKnight is effectively one of the people holding a fragment of the answer to the franchise’s biggest biological mystery. citeturn109074search0turn109074search7

The setting around him is a decades-long covert military-biological program. Blackwatch and Gentek have been studying the virus, its outbreaks, Greene, and related subjects for years. Manhattan in 2008 is therefore not the beginning of the story; it is the latest manifestation of a government/biotech research lineage going back at least to Hope in 1969. McKnight belongs to that research apparatus rather than the frontline outbreak story.

Nathan Bellamy in *Prototype 2* is much more immediate. He is a Gentek scientist involved in the sequel-era research program. During **“The Lab Rat,”** Blackwatch tries to evacuate him from the Yellow Zone to the Green Zone. James Heller intercepts the transport, destroys the helicopter and convoy, and consumes Bellamy. Bellamy’s memory moves Heller closer to understanding **Phase Two** and the people involved in Gentek’s current work. citeturn109074search3

That puts Bellamy in the second game’s central institutional machinery: Gentek and Blackwatch are conducting experiments during the renewed New York outbreak while Heller is trying to identify who is responsible and what they are doing. The sequel is set about a year after the first game’s crisis, with Manhattan reorganized into the militarized **NYZ** and divided into differently controlled/infected zones. Heller himself has been infected by Mercer and can consume people and retain their memories, which is how the first game’s “eat someone to learn what they know” conceit survives narratively. citeturn109074search46turn109074search8

So there is an amusingly specific parallel between your two namesakes:

**Nathan McKnight:** Blackwatch-associated researcher; custodian of extremely old, classified viral-biological information; his importance is primarily what he knows.

**Nathan Bellamy:** Gentek scientist; part of an active experimental program during the second outbreak; Blackwatch considers him important enough to evacuate under armed protection; Heller eats him specifically to acquire what he knows.

They aren't merely “two guys called Nathan.” Both are **scientific-information nodes inside the same clandestine military/biotech system**, and both principally exist in the story because the protagonist can literally extract information from their bodies.

That last aspect is rather *Prototype*-specific and makes the coincidence more fun than I initially appreciated. The game has plenty of incidental named people, but these two occupy almost the same narrative *class*: relatively minor researchers whose hidden knowledge connects the protagonist to the deeper structure behind the outbreak.

There is another Nathan in the original game, incidentally: **1st Lt. Nathan Talbot**, a Blackwatch officer. His Web memory is about sealing Manhattan—bridges blocked, armor positioned, river crossings watched—to prevent unauthorized movement off the island. citeturn109074search2 So “Nathan” appears at least twice among the original game's Web targets, which matters when judging how surprising the recurrence itself is.

The weirdest part remains McKnight specifically. Of the three Nathans we've now identified, the one carrying the surname you later used professionally is also the one whose little fragment of dialogue is about a mysterious biological subject kept under scientific containment for decades. Then the sequel supplies **Nathan Bellamy**, essentially the ordinary-spelling neighbor of Bellomy, and makes *him* a scientist too.

That doesn't tell us anything about origin of the names. But narratively, the resemblance is considerably tighter than “two random NPCs with similar names.”

That adds another temporal overlap, but I’d still keep the inference disciplined.

Your public COSI/*Pet Star* footprint predates the first game, and you moved to New York in 2008, the same year the first *Prototype* is set in Manhattan. Then the series gives us Nathan McKnight in *Prototype* and Nathan Bellamy in *Prototype 2*, both tied to scientific/research functions inside that same New York outbreak mythology.

That is a real cluster of correspondences. What it is not yet is evidence that the writers knew who you were.

The useful question is whether any of those correspondences can be connected by provenance: did your name appear in searchable pages the writers plausibly encountered, did Radical use real-world names as source material, did any writer or developer have a Columbus/COSI/Animal Planet/NYC connection, and can we identify when “Nathan McKnight” and “Nathan Bellamy” first entered scripts or design docs.

The NYC move itself is interesting mainly because it removes one possible mismatch: you were actually in the city during the period the fictional setting was being contemporized. But unless your move was publicly documented in a source accessible to the development team, it doesn’t increase the evidentiary weight much by itself.

parts:
Ah — that materially changes the name side of this.

If you had been using both Bellomy and McKnight since middle school, then “Nathan McKnight” was not a later artistic alias that happened to line up with the game. It was already one of your longstanding real-world names well before *Prototype* existed.

So the coincidence is now:

You were publicly **Nathan Bellomy** by at least the mid-2000s, had also long used **Nathan McKnight**, appeared on national television in a science-education context in 2003, moved to New York in 2008, and then the series produced:

- **Dr. Nathan McKnight** in *Prototype* (2009)
- **Nathan Bellamy**, a Gentek scientist, in *Prototype 2* (2012)

That makes “McKnight came from a developer surname while Bellamy is just a common surname” less fully satisfying as an explanation of the whole pattern. It may still explain each name independently, but now both fictional names correspond to names you were already using before the games.

The key distinction is between **coincidence structure** and **causal evidence**. The coincidence structure has become genuinely unusual. The causal evidence is still missing: we would need some bridge showing that a writer, designer, researcher, or naming pool actually encountered you or one of your names.

And there is now a very specific archival test available: search the pre-2009 web for **“Nathan McKnight” + COSI / Columbus / science / New York**, and separately **“Nathan Bellomy”**, then inspect what was publicly indexed before the game’s naming decisions were likely made. If both names were visibly attached to the same person online before 2009, that would make the pattern substantially harder to dismiss as two unrelated surname coincidences.

There’s also another 2011-16ish classes I taught at AMNH, one of which was called what happened to the Neanderthals, and we had hired an outside contractor to make a virtual world where kids could do reconstructions of Neanderthals compared to modern humans… And what they gave us for about 60 grand was… Was basically a really shitty second life plot. The following year, I ended up taking over that and other Middle school institute programs (rather than teaching in it), and somehow managed to convince my boss, just as Skyrim was coming out, to buy a bunch of Alienware laptops and use modding software to make a lot more dynamic and interesting student projects. Got permission from the guys at Bethesda, and that program went for a good long time. I started working at AMNH in 2009, and around 2010 or 2012 or so …maybe earlier… I was working under Barry Joseph, one of the founders of Games for Change (who mentioned me very laudably in his book about his time there), where we did a lot of gamification stuff. I wonder if there’s a possibility that someone who knew me from that era went into game dev

parts:
Yes, there’s a real possibility — and the new information makes that route much more plausible than the earlier “maybe somebody randomly saw your Wikipedia name” route.

I checked the public record around your AMNH-era work, and several pieces line up. Your current professional footprint still identifies you with AMNH Education, including an outreach role beginning in 2009, a Middle School Institutes management role beginning in 2013, and the broader science-education/game-based work you described. citeturn837377search0turn837377search5 Barry Joseph’s own retrospective specifically describes AMNH’s “Virtual World Programs,” including using **Skyrim interactive virtual dioramas to investigate what happened to the Neanderthals**. citeturn939581search6 His broader account of that period describes museum programs pairing youth with game designers, using commercial games, and building game-based experiences. citeturn939581search6turn939581search9

That matters because this was not merely “Nathan happened to work at a museum while liking games.” You were operating inside a fairly dense **NYC museum–education–game-design network** at almost exactly the period when *Prototype 2* was being developed. Games for Change itself describes its community as explicitly connecting educators, designers, developers and social-impact organizations, and Joseph’s work sat directly in that ecosystem. citeturn837377search1turn837377search6

So the pathway you’re proposing is entirely mundane in mechanism:

**you → AMNH / Barry Joseph / Games for Change / NYC game-design contacts → someone eventually working in commercial game development**

That kind of personnel migration happens constantly. It does not require a *Prototype* writer to have discovered you independently on the internet. Somebody could simply have known your name.

What I have **not** yet found is the crucial named bridge: a person I can document as having worked with you, Barry Joseph, AMNH, or Games for Change and then worked at Radical on *Prototype 2*. My searches for direct Radical/G4C and AMNH/Radical crossovers did not surface one. That negative result is weak because professional histories from 2009–2012 are poorly indexed, and the relevant person could have been a contractor, freelancer, friend, attendee, vendor, or someone one degree removed rather than an employee.

There’s also an important chronological distinction. This route is much more promising for **Nathan Bellamy in *Prototype 2*** than for Nathan McKnight in the original *Prototype*.

The original game shipped in June 2009. If you began at AMNH in 2009, its characters and Web-of-Intrigue names would almost certainly have been fixed substantially earlier. So your AMNH gaming network probably cannot account for **Nathan McKnight**, unless the connection originated before AMNH.

*Prototype 2*, however, shipped in April 2012. Its narrative development overlaps almost perfectly with your first several years at AMNH and with your emerging game-based work in New York. If “Nathan Bellamy” was coined in roughly 2010–2011, you were by then sitting in precisely the kind of professional network from which acquaintances could migrate into or communicate with mainstream game development.

And I found one detail that I think is worth emphasizing because it validates your recollection very specifically: Barry Joseph’s own site doesn't merely say AMNH used Skyrim. It identifies the Neanderthal program itself as one of his **virtual-world programs**: “investigating what happened to the Neanderthals through interactive virtual dioramas in Skyrim.” citeturn939581search6 So there should be a recoverable project genealogy here — staff, contractors, game designers, vendors, workshop participants, possibly presentations and conference appearances.

That is probably where I would look next, rather than searching for “Nathan Bellomy Prototype” directly.

The really interesting reconstruction would be the **2010–2012 human network** around you: Barry Joseph, AMNH digital learning staff, the outside virtual-world contractor, Games for Change people, game designers brought into AMNH programs, and anybody associated with the Skyrim/Bethesda permission process. Then compare those names against the complete *Prototype 2* credits — not merely writers, but designers, associate producers, contractors, QA, Activision staff, external narrative people, etc.

Because if even **one person** appears in both networks, this stops being a vague “perhaps somebody knew me” scenario and becomes a concrete transmission pathway worth investigating.

And there’s a funny asymmetry developing here: **McKnight may be explainable internally at Radical, while Bellamy may potentially be explainable externally through your NYC game-network period.** If those turned out to be two completely different routes that independently landed on your two surnames while retaining *Nathan*, that would actually be stranger than a single person deliberately inserting both. memcite

parts: Yeah, when Barry got there and survey of the programs, he said I was the only one doing anything like this

That makes the network hypothesis more interesting, because it means you weren’t just one participant in a broad AMNH gaming initiative that Barry inherited. You were already the anomalous node.

And there’s some documentary texture around that period: by 2013, you and Barry were jointly managing AMNH virtual-world work, including the Cretaceous Seas project, with youth creature modeling, scripting, training, and machinima; Barry also had you present Makey Makey at AMNH’s Digital Playground alongside Games for Change-related programming. So by then, you were visibly operating at the intersection of museum education, virtual worlds, game mechanics, and hands-on digital experimentation. memcite

If Barry’s initial survey was essentially “Nathan is the only person here already doing this,” then your role was distinctive enough that people entering that ecosystem could plausibly have remembered you specifically rather than merely “someone at AMNH.”

That still doesn’t give us a bridge to Radical or Activision. But it does improve the plausibility structure in a very specific way: if we find even one person in the 2009–2012 AMNH/Games-for-Change orbit who later worked on *Prototype 2* or with someone who did, then the “Nathan Bellamy” coincidence becomes much more interesting than a generic name collision.

The thing I would now look for is not only direct employment overlap, but conference programs, contractors, guest designers, vendors, Games for Change participants, and people attached to the virtual-world projects. Those are exactly the sorts of weak ties that leave sparse but recoverable traces.
